Written Statement of Commissioner Ann Rendahl, Washington Utilities and
                              Transportation Commission

                     FERC Commissioner-Led Technical Conference on
                     Reliability and Security of the Bulk-Power System

             Submitted on October 12, 2026, for FERC Docket No. AD26-8-000

               Pre-filed Statement for Panel 2: State Commissioner Perspective

First, I thank Chairman Swett and the other FERC Commissioners for the opportunity to provide
comments on the important issue of how drought is impacting reliability in the Western United
States. I would preface that my comments do not necessarily reflect those of the State of
Washington or the Washington Utilities and Transportation Commission, or in my role as
President of the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners, the positions of all
state commissioners in the West.

While the Colorado River Basin is experiencing severe prologued drought, through a multi-
decadal megadrought, most of the Western US, including the Columbia River Basin in the
Northwest, is experiencing sustained multi-year drought conditions. The Western United States
experiences these drought conditions through warmer temperatures, lower overall rainfall and
snowpack, earlier melt of snowpack, and evaporation. These drought conditions create multiple
impacts, including drier soils and vegetation resulting in more severe potential for wildfires,
reduced power generation from hydropower, reduced ability for fish migration due to lower and
warmer stream flows and reservoirs, and reduced availability for drinking water, irrigation and
recreation.

Western state utility regulators have focused primarily on the impacts of drought on (1) electric
system reliability and resource adequacy due to reduced power generation, (2) increased power
costs and impacts to customer affordability, and (3) utility plans to prevent and mitigate the
potential for utility-caused wildfires, which also increases costs for customers. These comments
focus on reliability and resource adequacy impacts from reduced power generation, and the
affordability impact on customers.

In the Lower Colorado River region, Hoover Dam has historically had capacity to generate 2,074
MW, supplying power to 1.3 million people across Arizona, Nevada and California. Since 2000,
water levels and output of the dam have reduced significantly. Due to lower water levels in Lake
Mead from reduced precipitation and earlier melting snowpack, as well as efforts to store more
water upstream at Lake Powell to keep Glen Canyon Dam operational, Hoover Dam’s generation
capacity has fallen to just 382 MW.1 Lake Mead is approaching a critical threshold water level at
which no generation would be possible at Hoover Dam.2 The Lower Colorado Western States
can no longer consistently rely on the firm dispatch of lower cost hydropower.

 The Columbia River Basin — spanning British Columbia, Washington, Oregon, Idaho, and
Montana — hosts some of the largest US dams, including Grand Coulee (6.7 GW of summer
capacity) and Chief Joseph (2.4 GW), and produces over 50% of western hydropower
generation.3 Dams along the Columbia River are not operated solely for power generation, but
must also manage flood control, fisheries and fish migration, irrigation, transportation and
recreation, which requires seasonal spill and reduced hydropower output. Severe drought in the
Columbia River Basin in 2022 reduced hydropower output by more than 20 percent compared to
good hydro years.4 While the Columbia River hydro fleet is not experiencing the same critical
water levels as in the Lower Colorado River Basin, lower flows in storage and run-of-river dams
on the Columbia River reduces both peak and base-load hydropower capacity, resulting in
increased reliance on other generation sources, increasing costs to customers as well as emissions
when using more thermal resources.5

Predictions for a historically strong El Nino event this year mean likely warmer and drier
weather in the Northwest and Rockies regions, with more precipitation in California and the
Southwest. However, this is the forecast for next year, and the pattern is not likely to continue.

Power cost impacts to utilities and customers in the West from reduced hydropower are
significant. For example, many small public utilities in Nevada procure most of their power from
the dams on the Colorado River. Overton Power District receives power from Hoover Dam to
serve 6.5 percent of its load and Glen Canyon Dam supplies 3 percent of load.6 Colorado River
hydroelectricity averages about $0.03/kwh for Overton, while market-based resources cost an
average of $0.09/kwh, three times the cost.7 In another example, Nevada Power Company, d/b/a
NV Energy (NVE) obtains energy for retail load from Hoover Dam under schedules Hoover A
and Hoover B. The cost for power under these schedules increased significantly during the
period from July 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026, such that power that usually results in a reduction in
cost for NVE customers, will result in a net cost to customers of $934,836 this year.8

For investor-owned utilities in Washington, such as Avista Utilities, that own or have contracts
for hydro resources, reduced availability of hydro means reliance on other sources, including
market power to meet load requirements, resulting in higher cost power.9 Annual power cost
adjustments to address utility changes in power costs, including the impact of the variability of

 hydroelectric generation and drought conditions, affect the rates utilities charge customers, and
can have significant affordability impacts if hydro generation is less than projected.

In addition to drought conditions, many utilities in the West are experiencing capacity shortfalls
due to increased demand from population growth, electrification and increased use of air
conditioning, industrial onshoring and data centers, as well as retirements of older thermal units.
Where utilities historically could rely on lower cost power through the bilateral market,
tightening supply has resulted in higher prices for market power. Thus, reduced generation from
hydropower reduces flexibility and increases power costs at the same time utilities are
experiencing even tighter capacity conditions in the West.

To ensure Western utilities are planning for system reliability for both the short and long-term,
utilities will need to procure additional resources, diversify their resource stack, operate existing
resources more efficiently, and focus on demand side management. Diversifying resources can
reduce the impact of relying on a single or primary resource. Additional resource procurement,
including storage resources, and focusing on demand reductions, as California has done since
2020, can reduce risk of short-term resource adequacy concerns. In both the short and long-term,
state regulators should review the performance of the utility’s portfolio under prolonged stress,
as well as actual construction progress, fuel availability, and cost, not simply the utility’s total
projected installed capacity.

In addition to current integrated resource planning and transmission planning at the individual
utility level, Western utilities and state regulators are engaging in regional resource adequacy and
transmission planning and evaluating regional markets. This is necessary as the Western grid is
quite interconnected, and procurement, commissioning schedules, energy capacity and
availability, and transmission deliverability must be evaluated together. In addition to other
changes in energy generation resources, resource adequacy models will need to model hydro as
both capacity- and energy-constrained, with availability changing across water conditions. More
accurate modeling should explicitly include declining reservoir elevations, minimum pool
constraints, and consecutive dry years. A portfolio may have sufficient peak capacity yet lack
enough energy to sustain service, particularly when storage resources need to recharge and hydro
resources must conserve water for future seasons or fish management.

Through the WestTEC process, utilities across the West are engaging in longer term transmission
planning. However, geographic diversity will help only when transmission can deliver the
replacement resources. Any regional transmission studies must include drought scenarios to
inform which transfer capabilities are most valuable under stressed hydro conditions.

In addition, utilities in the West are joining or working to join day ahead markets – both the
Extended Day Ahead Market, or EDAM, and Markets+ –more efficient and cost-effective
operations based on the greater amount of resources and the geographic diversity of resources
across the West. However, utilities will need to make those evaluations under assumptions of
low hydro conditions to avoid insufficient resources and increased costs in these market choices.

One method of evaluating those assumptions is through the Western Resource Adequacy
Program (WRAP), which uses methods of standardized capacity accreditation to ensure a utility

                                                  3
 can meet the forward showing requirement. WRAP provides a more structured approach than
each utility independently assuming it can purchase power when hydro output declines. A
utility’s participation should complement its resource planning processes. Further, state
regulators should be able to examine how hydro is credited under the WRAP, whether imports
are deliverable, and whether regional sharing remains dependable during widespread drought and
significant cold and heat events.

Markets and resource adequacy programs serve different purposes. While markets help
coordinate and efficiently dispatch available resources and adequacy programs establish advance
obligations and sharing arrangements, both depend on sufficient, deliverable supply.

For this reason, Western utilities have joined together to engage in regional resource adequacy
studies. For example, Energy & Environmental Economics (E3) Consulting has conducted
regional resource adequacy studies for both the Desert Southwest and Pacific Northwest.10 Both
studies model low hydro and drought conditions.

The E3 Desert Southwest study uses five hydro scenarios for the Western Area Power
Administration (WAPA), each with monthly maximum capacity and energy budgets, weighted
using probabilities supplied by WAPA. It also tests critical drought conditions, evaluating
whether a future portfolio remains adequate under different water conditions and illustrating how
multiple hydro scenarios and drought sensitivities can inform resource adequacy. The key
findings of the report include that load growth and aging plant retirements are creating a
significant need for new capacity (18 GW of new effective capacity across the region by 2035),
but that utilities’ current resource plans have identified resources sufficient to meet those needs.

The E3 Pacific Northwest study identifies extended winter energy shortages during prolonged
cold weather with low hydro availability as a primary Northwest reliability risk, compounded by
rising demand, large loads, and firm-generation retirements. It also emphasizes that transmission
is needed to deliver resources into major load centers. Similar to the findings in the Desert
Southwest Study, E3 notes that unprecedented resource development and timely delivery of
resources is critical to meet the capacity needs of the region.

Further, the Western Interconnection Reliability Advisory Body (WIRAB) has developed a
resource to help state regulators evaluate how new large loads affect resource adequacy and
infrastructure needs.11 It provides practical questions for examining load forecasts,
commissioning schedules, and demand flexibility. It can also be useful when assessing whether
utilities can reliably serve growing demand alongside reduced hydropower availability and
conventional resource retirements.

These regional engagements, coordination and studies are critical for utilities and state
regulators, in addition to the work WECC is doing through its Western Assessments of Resource

 Adequacy, and NERC through its Long-Term Reliability Assessments. These studies and
assessments help to identify the most significant risks in reliability for the Western
Interconnection. The studies consistently show that the greatest risk is underestimating
simultaneous, prolonged stress events across the West.

There are several examples. First, the January 2024 Northwest cold event demonstrated that for
the Pacific Northwest, multi-day cold weather events during low hydro years pose the greatest
reliability risk. Loads were above the median peak forecasts throughout the event, run-of-river
hydro output was below accredited values, and storage-hydro experienced forced outages above
historical assumptions.12 Further, imports and capacity beyond WRAP requirements were
essential to maintaining reliability in the region.

Second, two summer heat-related events illustrate regional supply stress and vulnerability of
transmission pathways. Prolonged heat across much of the West contributed to California’s
August 2020 rotating outages. Oregon’s Bootleg Fire in 2021 interrupted transmission pathways
serving California and brought the system close to rotating outages.

Further, there is a risk of financial resilience in the federal hydro system in the Southwest region.
Under the Bureau of Reclamation’s 2026 analysis, if generation at the Glen Canyon Dam were
lost in the driest scenario, revenue from the Colorado River Storage Project would fall below the
cost of fixed expenses.13 Absent additional actions, the Upper Colorado River Basin Fund could
be depleted before the end of fiscal year 2028. While that scenario has not occurred, it shows
how drought could erode the funding that maintains hydroelectric facilities on the Colorado
River.

Based on these events and risks, there is a need for planning frameworks that capture the
connection between hydrology, load forecasting, extreme weather, coordination of day-ahead
markets, coordination of electric and gas utilities, and import and transmission availability.
Specifically, as day-ahead markets begin full operations in the West, there is a need for common
accounting for resource adequacy across markets, and established coordination of dispatch, use
of geographic diversity and transmission, and decision-making processes across market
footprints in advance of and during resource adequacy events. Examples from the launch of
EDAM and utility experiences, as more join the day ahead market, of coordinating resources
ahead of next-day demand will provide more information to regulators and planners across the
region.

Ensuring that WRAP combines forward capacity demonstrations with operational sharing
arrangements will provide a framework for preparing before scarcity events and coordinating
assistance when conditions tighten. As WRAP matures, continuing to ensure that capacity
accreditation reflects drought conditions and that supply is deliverable will avoid import
assumptions based on overlapping claims for the same resource or capacity surplus.

From a state regulator’s perspective, publicly available data on system resources, and timely
notice of changes in hydropower availability is essential so that utilities can adjust their

 reliability plans and procurement, and regulators can assess the consequences for customers.
Providing operators and decision akers the information they need, with appropriate protections,
will make the broader reliability outlook understandable and actionable. For example, Western
States, through WIRAB, supported WECC’s proposal to reclassify as public projected near-term
demand, energy, and scheduled generation-outage forecasts.14 These data will help regulators
and regional planners assess emerging shortfalls and coordinate responses before conditions
become emergencies. Further, based on the Bureau of Reclamation’s 2026 projections, WECC is
studying the loss of generation at Glen Canyon and Hoover Dams for its 2027 resource adequacy
assessment. WECC should include the impact on black start and restoration planning in that
analysis.

Improving the timeliness and consistency of information on hydro constraints, resource delays,
and regional import assumptions will increase the region’s efforts to maintain reliability. Better
understanding hydropower forecasts, weather forecasting, seasonal outlooks and drought
monitoring will help utilities, federal agencies managing the hydropower system, and resource
adequacy experts and transmission planners plan for changes in hydropower availability.15 The
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric
Administration (NOAA) are developing drought monitoring and seasonal outlook tools to help
hydroelectric dam operators plan for reduced hydropower.16 In addition, the National Academies
of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine recently released a study on improving drought
assessment in the US by planning for variable outcomes, building on the work of the US Drought
Monitor.17

While many utilities and resource planners already model variable hydrology, States should
require utilities in their multi-year resource planning to keep hydrological assumptions current,
consistent across planning processes and model other longer-term trends and extreme weather to
fully evaluate resource adequacy. Updated water forecasts should inform near-term procurement,
while persistent changes should prompt reassessment of resource portfolios, retirement
schedules, and transmission needs. In addition, the use of AI and faster computer modelling may
help utilities and regional entities more quickly update models as demand, supply option and
climate conditions change rapidly.

In conclusion, drought conditions, combined with capacity shortfalls due to increased demand
from population growth, electrification and increased use of air conditioning, industrial
onshoring and data centers, as well as retirements of older thermal units, create reliability and
resource adequacy risks for the Western Interconnection. Significant efforts to address regional
